segs.text: Section nine. The historical examples, butyrylcholinesterase and N acetyltransferase two. These were the first metabolizing enzymes in which polymorphisms were studied. Neither handles many drugs, but their genes were worked out early and a few drugs tie clearly to them.

Butyrylcholinesterase hydrolyzes succinylcholine, a short acting muscle relaxant used in anesthesia that paralyzes muscles, including the diaphragm. An extensive metabolizer clears it in about two minutes, so breathing returns quickly. A slow metabolizer keeps it two to three hours and cannot breathe that whole time unless the exposure is known. The slow phenotype is rare, about one in three thousand patients.

N acetyltransferase two acetylates isoniazid, a tuberculosis drug, and procainamide. Patients are slow or fast acetylators, and both carry risk. Slow acetylators keep isoniazid around and get peripheral nerve damage; on procainamide they can get drug induced lupus, because the drug is not acetylated fast enough. Fast acetylators make more of the isoniazid metabolites that damage the liver, hepatotoxicity. So you cannot assume only one phenotype is dangerous.

The phenotypes differ by population. About thirty to forty five percent of Caucasians are fast acetylators. About ten percent of Japanese people are slow. About eighty percent of the Middle Eastern group are slow, so that is the group to watch for slow acetylator problems.
